items.content: The whistle came first, low and mournful, threading itself through the dark like something half-remembered. Then the rhythmic clatter of wheels against iron rails, rising and falling on the night air as the train moved through the valley below. She lay still beneath the sheets, listening as it swelled and faded, carrying with it the suggestion of other cities, other lives, platforms lit by yellow light where strangers stood with their luggage and their reasons. By the time silence returned, it felt heavier than before.

items.content: The streets looked smaller than memory had kept them, the oak tree at the corner somehow both ancient and diminished, as though the years had compressed it. She walked slowly, dragging her fingers along the familiar iron fence, half-expecting the past to rise up through the rust and meet her. Instead, there was only the strange doubling of it — the town that existed, and the town she had carried inside her all this time, overlapping imperfectly, like two transparencies held to the light.

items.content: The forest exhaled after the storm, a slow, deep breath that carried the smell of wet bark and crushed leaves through the cooling air. Water still moved everywhere — dripping from branch to branch, trickling down moss-covered trunks, pooling in the hollows of roots — though the sky had gone quiet and pale above the canopy. She stood without moving, her boots dark with mud, listening to the world settle back into itself like a sleeping animal finding its position.
